title: Fourth Homily on the Day of the Dormition

sections.heading: How many deaths has a man?

pairs.en: How many deaths has a man? One, people usually say — the one no man can escape. True: a man has one bodily death, which cannot be escaped. But there are two other deaths, which can and must be escaped. Since both of these deaths depend on us — and, if escaped, they place a man in the most blessed of states, while, if not escaped, they make him wretched for all eternity — it would seem there is nothing we ought to think about so often, nothing we ought to be so concerned about, as escaping these deaths. Yet see how careful we are! Many do not even know they exist!

sections.heading: The first death: the death of the soul

pairs.en: The first of these deaths is spiritual death, which consists in the deadening of the soul to life in God. It is produced by sin and lawlessness. Every sin is a sickness of the soul, a wound of the heart. But if these ailments, these wounds, are multiplied and left to fester, then at last comes the death of the soul: it becomes dead to God, to eternity, to virtue, to the law. Such a man, like a corpse, has the eyes of the mind, but does not see the light of God; he has hearing, but does not heed either the cry of poverty or the voice of justice; he has hands, but does not stretch them out to do good works; he has feet, but cannot take a single step on the path of repentance and amendment.

And our own eye sometimes sees this inner death — sees the state the soul is in. We say: “this is a soulless man”; “he has no conscience”; “he is heartless.” But all our expressions fall far short of the reality. No — this is a spiritual corpse. Inside such a man, as in a grave, there is death and decay: the decay of thoughts, of desires, of lusts! And perhaps, if we could see the soul in its inner condition, we would run from it in horror, as we would run from a dead man in the night.

Why, then, does such a man himself not feel his pitiful condition? Because he has lost the very faculty of spiritual feeling. This is precisely the mark of spiritual death — for a corpse feels nothing.

“But there is still feeling in him — after all, he thinks, desires, acts, enjoys, suffers.” Of course there is; but this is the feeling not of the spirit but of the flesh, a feeling wholly bent on bartering away eternity; it is the feeling not of a man but of the animals, for they too have their kind of sense — they desire, they enjoy, they suffer. Moreover this feeling — or, if you prefer, this remnant of feeling — is wholly taken up with fleshly vanity, wholly bent on trading eternity away: for one man, in exchange for honours; for another, for wealth; for another, for the pleasures of the senses. To this feeling, spirit and conscience are of no concern.

There are moments when this spiritual corpse — since grace never abandons even the last and least of sinners, and grace is all-powerful — seems, in those moments, to rise from the dead. He himself feels his terrible condition and does not hide it from others. Hence such expressions as: “I have hell in my soul”; “I am a man of perdition!”

These moments are the extraordinary moments of a life. In them the sinner, by the power of grace, is lifted, one might say, out of the depths of hell, raised to the midpoint between hell and heaven, and given the possibility of choosing once again the one or the other. Such moments become moments of conversion and spiritual resurrection, as soon as the sinner, coming to his senses, gives himself over to holy faith and repentance; and equally, these moments become moments of despair and suicide, when the dark power gains the upper hand in the sinner's soul over his awakened conscience.

Such is the death of the soul! It does not frighten us, because it is not so visible and hides itself under the covering of bodily life; yet it is the most terrible of all, for it alone makes bodily death a real evil for a man. Without the death of the soul, bodily death is even a great good, for it frees a man from the sorrows of this present life and delivers him into the land of peace and blessedness. Spiritual death is terrible also because it — and it alone — produces eternal death.
